notes.meaning: Jesus warns that things will come along that trip people up and lead them into sin. In a broken world this can't be avoided, but that is no excuse for the person who causes it. A "stumbling block" is like the trigger stick of a trap. The "little ones" are weak or young believers. It would be better to drown with a heavy millstone tied around your neck than to lead one of them away from Christ.

"Watch yourselves" means be careful. Don't trip others up, and don't lash out when someone wrongs you. If a fellow believer wrongs you, go to him directly and tell him kindly. When he repents, which means he is truly sorry and turns from the wrong, forgive him fully. Even if it happens again and again in one day, keep forgiving.

The apostles felt how hard this was. Forgiving again and again, and never causing others to fall, seemed beyond them. So they asked Jesus to make their faith stronger. They went to the right person, because Jesus is the one who grows our faith.

Jesus answers that even tiny faith, as small as a mustard seed, can do amazing things. The mulberry tree had huge, deep roots and was very hard to pull up. Telling it to be planted in the sea is a picture of doing what seems impossible. What matters most is not how much faith you have, but that it rests on God.

Jesus tells a short story about a servant, really a slave, coming in from a long day in the field. His master does not sit him down to eat first. The servant is expected to cook and serve, and to eat afterward. The master does not owe him special thanks for doing his job. In the same way, God owns us and all we do, so our service never puts Him in our debt.

So when we have done all God asks, we should say, "We are unworthy servants; we only did our duty." Our service adds nothing to God and earns us no credit with Him. Yet in His grace God still promises to reward His servants. That reward is a gift, not wages He owes us.

differ.view: The word here is "unprofitable," not "sinful." So this verse does not prove that Christians must keep on sinning. It means that even perfect obedience adds nothing to God.
Christ is describing a full keeping of God's law that no one actually reaches. Even our best obedience falls short and is mixed with faults, so no one can claim merit.

notes.meaning: Jesus was traveling toward Jerusalem. He went along the border between Samaria and Galilee. Few people knew Him in that area. Matthew Henry thinks He went that way to find these lepers.

Ten men with leprosy met Jesus. Leprosy was a skin disease that made a person "unclean" under Jewish law. The law made them live apart and keep their distance, so they shouted from far away. They called Him "Master" and begged for mercy. Shared misery had brought Jews and a Samaritan together, and our own sin should make us just as humble when we come to Christ.

Priests were the ones who examined a healed leper and declared him clean. Jesus sent the men to them before they were healed, so going was a real step of faith and obedience. As they went, they were made clean. God often meets us with mercy while we are obeying Him.

One man saw that he was healed and turned back. He praised God loudly and fell face down at Jesus' feet to thank Him. Luke adds that he was a Samaritan. Jews looked down on Samaritans, so he was the person least expected to give thanks.

Jesus noticed who was missing. All ten were healed, but only this "foreigner" came back to give glory to God. Ingratitude is very common, and few people who receive God's kindness stop to thank Him. Often the people we least expect turn out to be the most grateful.

Jesus told the man to get up and go on his way, probably to the priest as the law required. "Your faith has made you well" means more than a healed body. The other nine were cured on the outside, but this man also received a deeper, spiritual blessing. Calvin says he was welcomed among God's children.

The Pharisees asked when God's kingdom would come. They may have asked to mock Him, and they expected an earthly kingdom full of outward glory. Jesus said the kingdom would not come with signs you can watch for, like a king's grand parade. God's kingdom, His rule as King through the Messiah, comes quietly.

No one will be able to point and say, "Here it is!" God's kingdom rules in the heart and changes people from the inside. It was also right there among them, because Jesus the King stood in their midst. Older Bibles say "within you," while many read it as "among you." Both ideas appear in the older commentaries.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some today take this to mean that a seed of God's kingdom, something divine, lives inside every person.

notes.meaning: Jesus turned to His disciples. Hard days were coming when they would long for even one day like the ones they had spent with Him, but they would not get it. Trouble, persecution and waiting for His return lay ahead. We should treasure the good days of the gospel while we have them.

People would say, "Look, the Messiah is here!" or "There He is!" Many false messiahs did rise up, and more would come. Jesus says not to run after them. He will not be found tucked away in one special place.

When Jesus comes on His day, it will be like lightning flashing across the whole sky. It will be sudden and seen everywhere at once, not a secret in some corner. Wesley takes "His day" to mean the last day. Matthew Henry also sees here the gospel spreading quickly to all nations.
But first, Jesus must suffer many things and be rejected by the people of His own time. The cross comes before the crown. His followers should expect to suffer for Him too.

In Noah's day, people went on with normal life: eating, drinking and getting married. These things were not wrong in themselves. Their problem was that they ignored God's warning and were not ready. Then the flood came suddenly and swept them all away, and it will be the same when the Son of Man comes.

Lot's day was the same. The people of Sodom were busy buying, selling, planting and building. The very day Lot left, God sent fire and burning sulfur from the sky and destroyed them all. Jesus treats these Old Testament events as real history.

So it will be when the Son of Man is revealed. Careless people will be caught by surprise. Matthew Henry and others see this first in the fall of Jerusalem to the Roman armies, and finally when Christ returns to judge the world. So believers should always stay watchful.

On that day there will be no time to go back for your belongings. Someone up on the roof should not go inside for his things. Someone working in the field should not go home. Nothing in this world is worth the delay.
Lot's wife was led out of Sodom, but she looked back with longing, and she became a pillar of salt. Jesus warns us not to look back with yearning at what God calls us to leave behind.
Whoever clings to his life by turning away from Christ will lose it. Whoever is willing to lose his life for Jesus will keep it. He gains life that lasts forever.

At that time, people side by side will be separated. Two will be in one bed, or two women will be grinding grain together; one is taken and the other left. The ready and the unready live close together now, but a moment is coming that will part them. Matthew Henry reads "taken" as taken to safety, while the other is left to the ruin. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown sees this at Jerusalem's fall, and most of all at Christ's return.
This verse is in the King James Version but is missing from the oldest Greek copies of Luke. It was probably copied in from Matthew 24:40. It means the same as verses 34-35.

The disciples asked where this would happen. Jesus answered with a common saying: where there is a dead body, the vultures gather. Wherever sin and spiritual rot are found, God's judgment will come. Matthew Henry also sees a hopeful side: wherever Christ is, His people will gather to Him.
